strengths: Novel conceptual contribution: reframes ad-hoc teamwork partner generation as a DCD/UED problem in partner-policy space, generalizing prior approaches (FCP, MEP, E3T) as special cases of a unified framework.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning five Overcooked-AI layouts, a diverse and adversarially constructed evaluation population (BRDiv, planning agents, hardcoded agents, worst-case agents), the harder OGC benchmark, thorough ablations, and a real human-subjects study — this breadth is unusual and strengthens the credibility of the claims.

The proposed variance-based learnability score is simple, requires no extra computation beyond sampling, and is shown empirically to be robust and competitive with more complex alternatives (Gauss-weighted, success-rate-based), providing useful insight for the UED/curriculum-learning community.

The human study is well-designed (double-blind, randomized order, validated survey with high internal consistency, appropriate non-parametric statistical tests with multiple-comparison correction) and shows UPD is preferred both by returns and subjective ratings (adaptiveness, human-likeness, reduced frustration).

Interesting qualitative findings such as emergent convention-breaking/symmetry-breaking behavior that arises organically from the learnability-driven curriculum without explicit design, and clear visualizations of how the curriculum adapts epsilon per layout.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, architecture details, compute requirements, and hyperparameter search ranges provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The human study, while carefully executed, has a small sample (12 participants, 36 games per method across only 3 layouts), which limits generalizability and statistical power despite reaching significance; a larger and/or layout-more-diverse study would strengthen the human-alignment claims.

The paper omits direct comparison against some of the population-based curriculum or open-ended methods cited in the related work (e.g., ROTATE, COLE, RACCOON) that are arguably closer competitors than FCP/MEP/E3T, leaving open whether UPD's gains hold against more recent SOTA baselines.

Baseline training budgets differ (FCP/MEP trained for 2x more environment steps than UPD, with per-layout learning-rate tuning), which, although explained as a fairness measure, complicates a clean comparison and could be read either way regarding UPD's claimed "single hyperparameter set" advantage.

The hand-constructed evaluation population (mixing BRDiv, planning heuristics, hardcoded agents, and random/stay agents) is somewhat ad hoc; its coverage of realistic human-like or truly novel partner behavior is not rigorously justified beyond citing precedent, which affects how representative the reported average returns are of general AHT performance.

On the more challenging OGC benchmark, JUPD's absolute performance still "lags behind" single-layout-trained baselines (as the authors note), suggesting the joint curriculum's benefit is real but limited in the hardest generalization regime.

The method is currently restricted to discrete action spaces and captures only a narrow slice of behavioral diversity (competence and per-action bias via Dirichlet masking); richer partner intentions/goals are left as future work, somewhat narrowing the immediate scope of the contribution.

The reproducibility statement references a code repository but the link/text is missing/truncated ("Our code is available under"), which is a minor but notable oversight for a paper emphasizing reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem (joint partner/environment curricula for ad-hoc teamwork) and provides one of the first attempts to unify UED-style learnability curricula with partner generation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across five Overcooked-AI layouts, the OGC benchmark, several strong baselines (SP, FCP, MEP, E3T), and two ablations, plus a double-blind human-subject study with appropriate statistical corrections (Holm-Bonferroni, Wilcoxon, paired t-tests) and a reported Cronbach's alpha for the survey instrument.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter tables, architecture descriptions, training curves, and infrastructure details are provided in the appendix.

Interesting qualitative findings, such as the emergence of convention-breaking behavior and layout-dependent adaptation of the mixture coefficient, which provide some mechanistic insight into why the method works.
The extension of SFL's learnability score to a CV^2 formulation for joint level-partner scoring is a reasonable and practical engineering contribution for combining UPD with existing UED pipelines.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is fairly incremental: the main algorithmic change over E3T is to sample the mixture coefficient epsilon uniformly rather than fix it, add Dirichlet-biased action masks, and apply top-K selection by return variance — a near-direct adaptation of existing SFL/learnability scoring (Rutherford et al. 2024; Monette et al. 2025) to the partner-generation setting rather than a fundamentally new idea. The framing as a 'new framework' and claims of being the 'first' method to unify AHT and UED somewhat overstate the degree of innovation relative to the straightforward combination of known components.

The ablation results (Table 1) show that 'UPD w/o ℓ' (i.e., no learnability scoring at all, just random sampling from the generator) already achieves the second-best results and is fairly close to full UPD, which undercuts the paper's central claim that learnability-driven curriculum selection is a key driver of performance; the main benefit appears to come mostly from the stochastic generator itself.

The evaluation population used for Overcooked-AI (random/stay agents, mixtures, hardcoded partial-task agents) is constructed by the authors and overlaps substantially in character with the kind of stochastic mixture/bias partners UPD is trained against, which could create a built-in advantage for UPD/E3T-style methods relative to population-based baselines (FCP/MEP) that are not exposed to this type of partner distribution during training; this raises concerns about evaluation fairness and potential circularity.

The human-subject study, while methodologically careful, is based on a small sample (n=12 participants, 3 layouts, single episode per agent-layout pairing, 36 episodes per method total), which limits statistical power and the reliability of the significance claims, especially given the within-subject single-trial design and potential order/learning effects despite randomization.

Claims that UPD requires 'no manual parameter tuning' are in tension with Appendix Table 4, which shows that a hyperparameter search was indeed performed for UPD (albeit over a shared range across layouts); the distinction from baseline tuning is more about scope (single set across layouts vs. per-layout tuning) than the complete absence of tuning, and this nuance is underplayed in the main text.

Computational overhead of UPD (generating and rolling out many candidate partners, N=10 rollouts per candidate out of thousands of generated candidates per training loop) is not clearly quantified in wall-clock terms relative to baselines, making it hard to assess whether the method is actually 'lightweight' as claimed.

The method is demonstrated only in a single simple grid-world domain family (Overcooked-AI/OGC) with discrete 6-action spaces and two agents; generalization to richer action/observation spaces or more than two agents is unverified, and this limitation, while acknowledged, meaningfully constrains the claimed significance of the contribution as a general framework.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem—robust ad-hoc teamwork without expensive pretrained populations—and proposes a conceptually clean unification of AHT and UED through the notion of partner-space curricula, with prior methods (FCP, MEP, E3T) framed as special cases of a more general partner-generation view.

The method is lightweight and simple to implement (stochastic mixing + Dirichlet-biased randomization + variance-based learnability scoring), and the paper clearly explains how it generalizes E3T's fixed-mixture approach into an adaptive curriculum.

Empirical evaluation is extensive: five standard Overcooked-AI layouts against a diverse and deliberately adversarial evaluation population (BRDiv, planning agents, hardcoded agents, worst-case agents), ablations isolating the contribution of bias masking and learnability scoring, a comparison of four different learnability score formulations, and an extension (JUPD) to the harder Overcooked Generalisation Challenge with procedurally generated levels.

The human-subject study is a clear strength: a within-subjects, double-blind design with 12 participants, standard survey instrumentation, appropriate statistical corrections (Holm-Bonferroni, Wilcoxon signed-rank, paired t-tests), and good internal consistency (Cronbach's α) reporting. UPD wins on both objective return and subjective ratings (adaptiveness, human-likeness, less frustration), which is a meaningful and rarely-seen validation of an AHT method with real humans.

Qualitative analyses (Figures 3, 4, 15-17) offer interpretable insights into what the curriculum is doing (dynamic epsilon selection per layout, emergent convention-breaking, learnability concentrating on intermediate-competence partners), adding some mechanistic understanding beyond just performance numbers.
Reproducibility materials are thorough: detailed hyperparameter tables, architecture descriptions, infrastructure/compute details, and hyperparameter search ranges are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The user study, while well-designed in protocol, is very small (12 participants, 36 games per method), which limits statistical power and the robustness of significance claims, particularly for the per-question Wilcoxon tests after multiple-comparison correction; a discussion of effect sizes or confidence intervals beyond significance stars would strengthen the claims.

The variance-based learnability score ℓvar as defined is maximized when returns are bimodal at 0 and Rmax, but Overcooked rewards are typically not binary/bimodal in practice; the ablation in Fig. 5 is helpful but the theoretical argument for why variance (vs. e.g. entropy of outcomes) is the right general objective in continuous-reward cooperative settings could be more rigorously justified or theoretically grounded rather than argued primarily by analogy to the binary SFL case.

No comparison is given against other adaptive/population-growing curriculum baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., Li et al. 2023's open-ended partner generation, Wang et al. 2025's ROTATE, or You et al. 2025's automatic curriculum design), which are arguably the closest competitors conceptually; only FCP, MEP, SP, and E3T are used as baselines, leaving open how UPD compares to other recent curriculum-based or open-ended AHT methods.

The JUPD experiments are restricted to a reduced 5x5 OGC grid for computational tractability, and the paper explicitly notes that OGC and Overcooked-AI results are not directly comparable due to observation differences, somewhat limiting the generality of the joint-curriculum claims to the harder, more realistic full-scale OGC setting.

The method currently only targets discrete action spaces and a narrow notion of behavioral diversity (competence mixing + per-action Dirichlet bias), as acknowledged by the authors; it's unclear how well the learnability-based curriculor generalizes to richer/structured partner diversity (e.g., goal- or intention-level diversity), which somewhat limits the claimed generality of the framework beyond the evaluated domains.

Statistical reporting for the main Overcooked-AI results (Table 1) lacks explicit significance testing between UPD and the strongest baselines (e.g., UPD w/o ℓ) across seeds, relying only on mean ± std comparison, which makes it harder to assess whether some per-layout gains (e.g., CRoom, FC) are statistically robust given overlapping standard deviations.

strengths: Extends the well-established unsupervised environment design (UED)/learnability paradigm to the partner space in ad-hoc teamwork, providing a clean population-free alternative to E3T that removes manual tuning of the mixture coefficient epsilon.

Very thorough empirical evaluation: LBF, five Overcooked-AI layouts, and the harder Overcooked Generalisation Challenge (joint partner-environment curriculum), plus a double-blind human-AI user study with proper statistics (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Holm-Bonferroni correction, Cronbach's alpha for internal consistency). The paper reports 282 trained policies in total, indicating substantial experimental effort.

Informative ablations (UPD w/o bias, UPD w/o learnability) and analyses of partner-selection dynamics (Figures 4-6) that provide mechanistic insight, including an interesting emergent 'convention-breaking' phenomenon analogous to hand-engineered methods like Other-Play.

Additional appendix material strengthens the submission: a formal computational-cost comparison against population-based methods, comparison with a recent strong baseline (ROTATE), sensitivity analysis over alternative learnability functions, and a transparency note explaining and correcting earlier bugs.

Human study results are consistent with automated evaluation, showing UPD is rated more adaptive, more human-like, and less frustrating, which strengthens the practical relevance of the claims beyond synthetic partner populations.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines an existing partner-generation mechanism (E3T's ego/random mixture) with an existing learnability-based curriculum objective (SFL/Monette et al.'s variance-based scoring), applied to a new axis (partners rather than levels). The conceptual leap, while clean, is a fairly direct transplantation of prior ideas.

The ablation 'UPD w/o learnability' performs nearly as well as full UPD in several Overcooked layouts (e.g., only clearly better in AA), suggesting that much of the benefit comes from large-scale randomized partner generation rather than the learnability mechanism itself, somewhat undercutting the central motivating claim about learnability-driven curricula.

The theoretical justification linking variance-based learnability to expected policy improvement relies on an external, not-yet-published result (Foster et al., 2026) that is asserted rather than derived or empirically validated within this paper.

UPD underperforms population-based/other methods on at least one layout (CRoom) and does not dominate uniformly, and the human study (n=12 participants) is small, which the authors themselves note limits claims of overall superiority.

The partner generator (Alg. 2) still involves hand-specified structural choices (mixture with random policy, Dirichlet-based bias masking, bias probability) — so while explicit mixture-coefficient tuning is removed, the framework is not entirely free of design choices, and its generality to richer/more realistic partner distributions (e.g., human-like biases beyond simple action Dirichlet biases) is untested.

Scalability beyond two-agent settings and beyond relatively simple discrete gridworld domains (LBF, Overcooked, small 5x5 OGC) is not demonstrated, leaving open questions about applicability to larger teams or more complex/continuous domains.

strengths: The paper is thorough in its empirical scope: three benchmark families (LBF, Overcooked-AI, OGC), multiple population-based and population-free baselines, ablations (w/o bias, w/o learnability), sensitivity analysis of the learnability function, a computational cost analysis, and a human-AI user study with proper statistical correction (Holm-Bonferroni).

The idea of extending unsupervised environment design's learnability principle from environment parameters to partner policies is a reasonable and clearly motivated conceptual step, and the paper explicitly connects it to recent theory relating learnability/return-variance to expected policy improvement.

The qualitative analyses (Figures 4-6, learnability-vs-return scatterplots, emergent convention-breaking) provide some mechanistic insight into why the method works, beyond just reporting aggregate numbers.
Reproducibility materials (hyperparameter tables, architecture details, compute budget discussion) are extensive.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely combinatorial rather than fundamentally new: the partner generator is an extension of E3T's mixture-policy idea with randomized epsilon and action-bias masking, and the selection criterion is a direct transplant of SFL/return-variance learnability from prior UED work (Rutherford et al. 2024; Monette et al. 2025). The paper's own appendix (Section J.1) shows that simply randomizing epsilon without any learnability scoring ('UPD w/o ℓ') already recovers most of the benefit, undercutting the centrality of the claimed learnability contribution.

The Transparency Note in Appendix B discloses that an earlier version had 'implementation and configuration issues affecting baseline experiments' that were later corrected. While the authors state conclusions were unchanged, this self-reported issue combined with the fact that baselines (MEP in particular) required per-layout hyperparameter tuning while UPD was mostly evaluated with a single fixed configuration (only shown to benefit further from fine-tuning in Appendix D) raises concerns about the fairness/rigor of the baseline comparisons.

The headline claim that UPD 'consistently achieves strong performance' is weaker than it appears on inspection: UPD underperforms other methods on CRoom in Table 1, and in the extended comparison (Table 3) ROTATE outperforms UPD on three of five layouts (CRoom, CR, FC), with UPD winning mainly in aggregate average — this nuance is understated in the abstract/introduction.

The evaluation partner population (BRDiv, hardcoded, planning agents) is constructed by the same authors' pipeline and partially overlaps with the partner-generation logic used to train UPD (mixtures of ego/random policies with biases), which raises the possibility of a favorable alignment between training and evaluation distributions that is not fully addressed.

The theoretical justification for using return variance as a learnability signal relies on citing an unpublished/forthcoming work (Foster et al., NeurIPS 2026) whose applicability to the specific partner-conditioned game setting is asserted rather than derived in the paper itself, making this a somewhat unverifiable claim of principledness.

The human study, while appropriately analyzed statistically, has only 12 participants and 36 games per method, and the authors themselves caveat that it demonstrates UPD's effectiveness rather than establishing it as definitively best; this modest sample size limits the strength of the human-AI claims relative to how prominently they are featured in the abstract.

OGC experiments are restricted to a reduced 5x5 setting for tractability, which limits the extent to which the joint partner-environment curriculum claims generalize to the full/harder version of the benchmark.

strengths: Clean conceptual contribution: extends unsupervised environment design (learnability-based curricula) to the partner space, unifying environment and partner generation under one adaptive, population-free framework (UPD/JUPD).

Extensive empirical validation across three benchmarks (LBF, Overcooked-AI, OGC) with 282 trained policies, multiple strong baselines (SP, FCP, MEP, E3T, ROTATE), and thorough ablations (w/o bias, w/o learnability) that isolate the contribution of each design choice.

Rigorous human-AI user study with double-blind design, ethics approval, appropriate statistical corrections (Holm-Bonferroni), and high measured internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha), showing UPD is preferred by humans on multiple subjective dimensions and achieves higher returns.

Insightful analysis of partner-selection dynamics (learnability vs. return plots, epsilon trends across layouts, emergent convention-breaking via directional action-bias switching) that provides interpretability beyond aggregate performance numbers.

Strong reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter tables, compute/runtime analysis with derived break-even population size formulas, described codebase lineage, and an honest transparency note about corrected baseline issues.

Practical significance: removes need for expensive pre-trained partner populations and manual mixture-coefficient tuning (a known limitation of E3T), while extending naturally to procedurally generated joint partner-environment curricula where population methods struggle to scale.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for using return variance as a learnability signal (subsection 4.1) leans heavily on an unpublished/forthcoming result (Foster et al., 2026, cited as a NeurIPS submission), which cannot be independently verified and weakens the rigor of the stated formal connection to policy improvement.

Performance is not uniformly dominant: UPD underperforms baselines on the Cramped Room layout in Overcooked-AI, and ROTATE outperforms UPD on several layouts (Appendix D), somewhat tempering the 'consistently strong' framing in the abstract/intro.

The convention-breaking argument in Section 4.4 is only formally derived for a toy 2x2 matrix game; while Figure 6 offers empirical support in full Overcooked layouts, the generalization from the toy analysis to complex multi-step coordination games is not rigorously established.

The human study, while well-designed, has a modest sample size (12 participants, 36 games/method), which limits statistical power and the strength of claims about human-likeness and adaptivity despite reported significance.

The 'no manual tuning' selling point is partially undercut by the fine-tuned UPD variant (Appendix D/E) that uses per-layout curriculum hyperparameters and outperforms the default UPD, suggesting that further gains are available through tuning that the main experiments intentionally avoid.
OGC experiments are restricted to a small 5x5 grid for tractability, leaving open how well the joint partner-environment curriculum scales to larger, more realistic procedurally generated settings.

A disclosed 'Transparency Note' indicates that an earlier version of the paper had implementation/configuration issues affecting baselines that were later corrected; while transparently reported, this raises some caution about the care needed in baseline tuning and residual risk of further undiscovered issues.
